articles.title: Cult of male genius holding female film-makers back, says Woman Unknown director
articles.summary: May el-Toukhy says we must end veneration of male directors that causes ‘structural problem’ for women. The enduring cult of male genius is keeping down female film-makers, one of the only two female directors in the running for the top prize at this year’s Venice film festival has warned.
body: “I’ve never ever read an article where a female director is promoted as a genius,” said the Danish-Egyptian director May el-Toukhy, whose film Woman Unknown has been selected for the Golden Lion competition on the Lido this year.
“It’s not that I think I am one, but it’s just interesting that this is so systemic,” she added. “All of us are responsible for changing that discourse.”

El-Toukhy’s post-second world war period drama was the only film by a woman in the main competition when the line-up was announced in July. Since then, the festival directors have added the documentary NAZA, which is co-directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian.
A competition prize at Europe’s top festivals, Cannes, Venice and Berlin, is seen as a major door-opener for films seeking distribution deals around the world.
points: May el-Toukhy says we must end veneration of male directors that causes ‘structural problem’ for women.

articles.title: Wim Wenders clarifies that he does not believe film-makers should stay out of politics
articles.summary: Director’s controversial comments earlier this year warned of films that ‘enter the field of politics’ The director Wim Wenders has clarified personal views on the relationship between cinema and politics that caused controversy earlier in the year, saying at the Venice film festival that he does…
body: During the Berlin film festival, the veteran German director, who was acting as the jury president, had said at a press conference that “we have to stay out of politics because if we make movies that are dedicatedly political, we enter the field of politics.”

The remark drew much attention amid criticism of the German government’s support of Israel over the war in Gaza, and incensed some fellow film-makers, with the Indian author Arundhati Roy calling the comments “unconscionable” and pulling out of an event in the German capital.
Asked by the Guardian at a press conference in Venice whether he stood by the comments, Wenders said he “could repeat the same thing” but conceded he “could be more explicit”.

“What I said then was, as film-makers, we are the opposite of politicians. We have empathy. Politics work without empathy; that’s all I said,” said the auteur, who had come to the Lido to present a documentary about the Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.

articles.title: ‘The Echo Chamber’ Review: Luca Marinelli, Alicia Vikander and Susan Sarandon Reverberate Through a Smoky, Somber Single-Location Love Story
articles.summary: If you’re ever thinking of attempting a single-location film, choose that location with care. Make it high-ceilinged, light-filled, book-lined, with a reading-nook conservatory area, a gargantuan sofa, a killer sound system and space enough that you don’t even have to turn sideways to sidle past…
body: Andrea Pallaoro's restrained realization of Bernardo Bertolucci's final screenplay features a strong cast in a subdued romantic drama about music, addiction, recovery and exquisite interior decor.

The film is certainly beautiful, shot in gorgeously rich Academy-ratio frames by Apichatpong, Reygadas and Refn collaborator Diego Garcia, who makes portraiture and still life out of every single closeup, and landscapes out of the different planes that can be achieved through the modular lighting and glass panels of Gaspare de Pascali’s exquisite production design. And, at least until a highly unnecessary eleventh-hour swerve into melodrama, it is directed with great sensitivity and restraint by Pallaoro, who has never once been guilty of overstatement across his three fine previous features: “Medeas,” “Monica” and “Hannah.”

articles.title: Box Office: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Remains No. 1 in Sixth Weekend, Nears ‘Avengers: Endgame’ All-Time Domestic Record
articles.summary: “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” was No. 1 at the domestic box office for the sixth consecutive weekend, a rare feat that underscores the movie’s remarkable staying power as well as the lack of competition on cinema marquees.
body: “This summer could signal a meaningful turning point for movie theaters,” says Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian. “More than anything, it serves as a huge reminder of the singular nature of the moviegoing experience and how much fun people have going to theaters.”

Unfortunately, summer is ending with a whimper rather than a bang. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” prevailed over several underwhelming new holiday releases, including Paramount’s R-rated crime thriller “ By Any Means,” Lionsgate’s anxiety-inducing sequel “Fall 2: Deadpoint” and A24’s action horror film “Onslaught.”

articles.title: At Telluride Film Festival, Bill Gates Compares Lack of Control Over AI to HAL in ‘2001’: ‘You Could Say “Please Shut Down,” and It Would Say, “OK, I Took That Under Advisement, But…”‘
articles.summary: Plenty of comparisons have been made in recent years between fast-developing artificial intelligence systems and HAL, the rogue computer in Stanley Kubrick’s “2001: A Space Odyssey” that operated by its own sets of rules, ultimately disregarding human oversight.
body: Gates invoked the alien movies of yore in which governments bandied together to solve the invasion threat, saying, 'Believe me, the aliens are here — a foreign intelligence with a different set of motivations that we can't even understand.'

“You know, there are these movies where the aliens are coming, and you see unprecedented levels of cooperation between specifically China and the U.S., where (it’s), ‘Oh my God, the aliens are coming!’ Well, believe me, the aliens are here — you know, a foreign intelligence with a different set of motivations that we can’t even understand. And so we need something almost surprising like that, in order to step up to it.”

“And ironically, we’re the ones that are birthing the aliens,” said another panelist, Tristan Harris, co-founder of the Center for Humane Technology, as Gates nodded. “So it’s actually within the full remit of the two countries to limit (uncontrolled growth of the tech), at least to the current level of alien intelligence that we’re at now.”

articles.title: Luc Besson Calls Madonna a ‘Phenomenon,’ Admits He’s Developing Another ‘Crazy’ Sci-Fi Story: ‘You Will Need a Ticket — And an Aspirin’
articles.summary: Luc Besson is writing another sci-fi story right now. “It’s going to be crazy, believe me. Maybe you will need a ticket and an aspirin at the same time. I’m older, so I’m trying to explore everything now,” he admitted during a masterclass at Venice Film Festival.
body: “This whole technical evolution … As a director, you just digest it. It’s always just a tool,” he said.
“I know lots of people are afraid of AI. But it’s a tool! Don’t be afraid. It’s a tiger — but you are a guy with a whip, speaking German to it.”

No stranger to Venice, Besson wrote and produced this year’s “ Father Joe,” directed by Barthélémy Grossmann. The film, which premiered out of competition, features Kiefer Sutherland as a priest fighting a crime boss played by Al Pacino.
Pacino missed the press conference for the film, instead sending a video message and praising Besson: “It’s great to say his name,” he said.

articles.title: French thriller Jupiter brings nuclear anxiety to red carpets of Venice
articles.summary: Director Alexandre Smia says film about Russia detonating nuclear warhead – and US refusing to respond – is not unrealistic. Russia has detonated a nuclear warhead over the Black Sea to underline its desire to revenge an assassination attempt on the Russian president.
body: A new thriller, which has brought nuclear anxiety to the red carpets of the Venice film festival this week, plays through what would happen next. In Jupiter, which premiered on the Lido on Friday, the duty to square up to the Kremlin and enter the stress-inducing mind games of the nuclear deterrent falls on the fictional French president Paul Archambault (played by the hulking French actor Denis Ménochet), who is backed in his mission by the British prime minister.
It’s a scenario that is far from unrealistic, the French film-maker Alexandre Smia said on the eve of his film’s premiere.

“Even if the US disengagement from Nato is not official, we have reason to doubt that the US would offer its nuclear umbrella if one European city were to be attacked nowadays,” said Smia, who has previously directed episodes of the French spy TV series Le Bureau des Légendes.

“And considering that France is the only country in Europe that is both a member of the European community, of the security council of the United Nations and of Nato, it naturally becomes actually the country where the responsibility of making decisions lies.”

body: Ye-ji intrusively pokes her camera into every corner of the couple’s lives. Mi-ok grasps how therapeutic it could be for them both to talk about their experiences and to have a kind of ownership of what they’ve been through; Ho-seok is much more reluctant to talk, partly because it has been so horrible – and also, perhaps, because he can see that comparing their humble lives to these wealthy people will be intimately painful and destructive.

articles.title: Pulp top the bill at 20th End of the Road Festival
articles.summary: The End Of The Road Festival near Blandford Forum sees a packed event with 15,000 visitors.
body: A sell-out crowd of 15,000 helped celebrate the End Of The Road Festival's 20th birthday this weekend, in one of the final events of the UK summer season.
Britpop luminaries Pulp closed the mainstage on Saturday night at the four-day event, near Blandford Forum, Dorset.
The event's anniversary line-up also included Irish indie-pop singer Cmat, New York art-rockers Geese and Canadian singer-songwriter Mac DeMarco.
More than 140 acts performed across the five music stages which showcased a mix of indie-rock, folk and alternative artists.

articles.title: 5 Star Trek: The Next Generation Episodes With Great Space Battles
articles.summary: Space warfare wasn't all that common on Star Trek: The Next Generation, but when it did happen, it left an impact. Here are the five best space battle episodes.
body: To put it on the record right away: "Star Trek: The Next Generation" isn't really a "space battle" kind of show. Creator Gene Roddenberry launched "Next Generation" in 1987 with the hopes of making it even more peaceful, egalitarian, and diplomatic than the original "Star Trek." He even instilled a strict policy of no interpersonal conflicts between the main characters, which, as you can imagine, frustrated the show's writers to no end.

The USS Enterprise-D may be equipped with powerful phaser banks and a full complement of photon torpedoes, but the ship rarely enters into any situation with weapons hot. Even when an enemy vessel appears directly in their path, the ship will merely go to yellow alert, and Captain Picard (Patrick Stewart) will calmly ask what it is they might want before taking any kind of tactical action. Yes, the Enterprise can fight off attackers, and Starfleet vessels are sometimes used to form blockades or provide weapons backup to tense situations, but it's rare that you'll see any of them firing the first shot.

articles.title: ‘Making Marie Antoinette’ Review: Eleanor Coppola’s Chronicle of Daughter Sofia Shooting Her 2006 Biopic Makes for a Sublime Collaboration of Talents
articles.summary: Premiering at Telluride, the doc will be pure catnip for fans of the Kirsten Dunst-starring film in all its candy-colored, New Romantic, defiantly anachronistic glory.
body: As explained by opening intertitles, the raw footage for this current film lay dormant for years after shooting, only parts of it used for Marie Antoinette ‘s marketing campaign at the time. Spending lockdown together in 2020, Eleanor and Sofia started organizing the material with a view to finally finishing it. After Eleanor died in 2024, Sofia pressed on to finish it as a tribute to her mother, and only Eleanor is given the director credit here (Sofia is listed as one of its producers).

Viewers may wonder at how much each filmmaker shaped the end product. But care has clearly been taken to ensure that Eleanor’s is the dominant voice, even if the voice we literally hear reading Eleanor’s diary entries from the time is actor Diane Lane’s. An early montage of shots where Eleanor can be seen reflected in the many mirrors of Versailles, holding her camera to her face, also helps to resuscitate her as a presence here.
